description: We are an interdisciplinary team: an astronomer, a biologist and three economists, working on “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars.” Our astronomer covers lunar and Martian conditions and coding, our biologist brings extremophiles and habitability, and our economists bring decision analysis and cost modeling. We don’t just ask where Earth looks like Mars, but where it’s the most practical to test.
summary:
We developed "The Moon on our Planet", an interactive website that identifies Earth locations reproducing measurable conditions of three candidate regions at the lunar south pole: Shackleton Crater, Malapert Massif and the Shackleton–de Gerlache Ridge.
The challenge asks for Earth analogs of future Moon base sites. Rather than looking for landscapes that merely resemble the Moon, we profiled each lunar target from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data, screened 15 Earth candidates, and scored them on seven weighted criteria with fixed numeric thresholds. The resulting lunar-similarity index stays stable under ±10% weight changes and is calibrated against well-known analogs. Four sites emerged, deliberately excluding the widely studied ones named in the brief: Scărișoara Ice Cave, Adventdalen, Askja and Mistastin Lake Crater, plus Dasht-e Lut as a process analog. For each we state what is similar, how similar it is, and where the analogy breaks down.
We also scored how practical each site is to reach and plotted similarity against practicality. This matters because testing instruments, rovers and crews on Earth is far cheaper than on the Moon — but only when the chosen site is both scientifically valid and genuinely reachable.
details:
What it does. The Moon on our Planet identifies places on Earth that reproduce specific, measurable conditions of three candidate regions at the lunar south pole: Shackleton Crater, Malapert Massif and the Shackleton–de Gerlache Ridge. Instead of looking for landscapes that simply look lunar, we compare parameters, rank the sites, and state openly where every analogy breaks down.

How it works. First we profiled the three lunar targets across eight parameters — geology, relief, temperature, illumination, water ice, dust, subsurface voids and working conditions — using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data (LOLA topography, Diviner temperatures, LEND hydrogen, Mini-RF radar, LROC imagery) through the NASA Planetary Data System. Then we screened 15 Earth candidates across eight environment types and scored each on seven criteria with fixed numeric thresholds: temperature regime, ice, relief, mineralogy, climate, voids and accessibility. Weights reflect what matters at the pole, with cold and ice highest at 0.20 each, producing a single lunar-similarity index. A programmatic sweep of all 14 weight variants at ±10% never changes the ranking, and we validated the scale against a control group of well-known analogs: Haughton Crater 3.00, Lanzarote 2.80, Atacama 2.20.

Results. Four sites and one additional process analog: Scărișoara Ice Cave, Romania (3.40), Adventdalen, Svalbard (3.35), Askja, Iceland (2.75), Mistastin Lake Crater, Canada (2.40), plus Dasht-e Lut, Iran as a thermal-fatigue analog. Scărișoara reproduces cold trapping, the physics that preserves ice in permanently shadowed regions; Mistastin is formed in anorthosite, the rock of the lunar highlands; Adventdalen offers ground ice and a permanently low Sun; Askja provides existing ground-penetrating radar data on buried ice.

Beyond the brief. Our team includes three economists, so we added a practicality index built from access, infrastructure, permits and season length, and plotted similarity against practicality. The matrix turns a scientific comparison into a testing plan: Adventdalen and Scărișoara for repeated low-cost campaigns, Mistastin for occasional well-prepared expeditions, Askja as a reference baseline.

Impact. Field testing on Earth is far cheaper than testing on the Moon. By naming sites that are both scientifically valid and genuinely reachable, the project helps direct instrument trials, rover tests and crew training toward locations where the effort pays off.

Tools. HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with no framework; SVG for the orthographic globe and charts, projected with d3-geo and Natural Earth outlines; the Web Audio API for a procedurally generated ambient soundtrack; Google My Maps for the interactive site map; Google Workspace for collaboration. Imagery comes from NASA archives and our own research files.

Creativity. We looked for processes, not postcards. We deliberately set aside the widely studied analogs named in the challenge brief, published the limits of each analogy next to its strengths, and combined planetary science with decision analysis drawn from our team’s mix of astronomy, biology and economics.
